market_context: United States and general English-speaking market
title: Peanuts vs. almonds: nutrition differences

seo.title: Peanuts vs. almonds: protein, fiber and minerals
seo.meta_description: Per 30 g, peanuts provide ~165 calories, 7.0 g protein and 2.4 g fiber; almonds ~175 calories, 6.5 g protein and 3.2 g fiber. Compare minerals too.
seo.search_intent: Compare peanuts and almonds for protein, fiber, fat, calories and minerals

excerpt: Peanuts and almonds are very similar in a realistic serving. At 30 g, raw peanuts provide about 165 calories, 7.0 g protein, 13.0 g fat and 2.4 g fiber; raw almonds about 175 calories, 6.5 g protein, 15.3 g fat and 3.2 g fiber. Peanuts edge ahead in protein, while almonds provide more fiber, calcium and magnesium.
content_html:
A peanut is botanically a legume and an almond is the seed of a drupe, but put 30 g of each on a plate and the nutrition profiles look surprisingly similar. The differences are real, but not nearly as dramatic as the botanical labels suggest.

Compare 30 g of both, raw

Per 30 gPeanutsAlmonds
Calories~165~175
Protein~7.0 g~6.5 g
Fat~13.0 g~15.3 g
Fiber~2.4 g~3.2 g
Magnesium~54 mg~77 mg
Calcium~15 mg~76 mg

Both rows use current USDA Foundation raw-food references and the food-specific energy calculation for a like-for-like comparison.

Protein: a small peanut advantage

Raw peanuts provide about 23.2 g protein/100 g and almonds 21.5 g. In a 30 g handful, the difference is less than 1 g.

Both can contribute protein, but neither becomes the equivalent of a large main-dish protein serving simply because the per-100-g number is high.

Fiber and minerals: almonds

Almonds provide about 10.8 g fiber/100 g versus 8.0 g in peanuts. They also contain much more calcium—about 254 versus 49 mg/100 g—and more magnesium, about 258 versus 180 mg.

Calories are in the same range

Thirty grams lands around 165–175 calories in these references. Claims that one is dramatically more fattening than the other usually disappear when the serving weight is equalized.

Preparation may matter more than the raw difference

Salt, frying oil, honey, sugar coatings or chocolate can shift the final nutrition more than the natural gap between the two foods. Salted oil-roasted peanuts should not be compared with plain raw almonds as if the base ingredient caused every difference.

For simple versions, choose by flavor, price and your target nutrient: slightly more protein from peanuts; more fiber, calcium and magnesium from almonds.

The protein difference is smaller than the food-category difference suggests

Peanuts are botanically legumes, while almonds are tree nuts, yet nutritionally they overlap enough to be compared in the same snack category. Peanuts usually provide a little more protein per ounce, whereas almonds tend to provide more vitamin E and calcium. Both supply mostly unsaturated fat, some fiber, magnesium, and substantial calories. The practical result is that neither is a universal winner; the better choice depends on which nutrients and eating pattern matter most.

Portion size is important because a small handful can contain around 160–180 calories. That is not a reason to avoid nuts or peanuts, but it explains why comparing them by “cups” can be misleading. A standard ounce makes protein, fat, fiber, and calorie differences easier to interpret.

Roasting and added ingredients can matter more than peanut versus almond

Dry-roasted, oil-roasted, salted, honey-coated, and chocolate-covered products are different foods nutritionally. Added salt can raise sodium sharply, while sugar coatings increase carbohydrate and calories without improving the core nutrient profile. If the goal is to compare the nuts themselves, plain or lightly salted versions give the cleanest comparison. Roasting may alter flavor and some heat-sensitive compounds, but both raw and roasted forms can be nutritious choices.

Nut butters follow the same principle. A peanut butter made from peanuts and perhaps salt differs from a product with added sugar and hydrogenated or palm fats. Almond butter is not automatically healthier simply because it is more expensive. Checking ingredients, sodium, added sugar, and serving size gives a more grounded comparison.

Allergy and affordability can decide the choice immediately

Peanut allergy is common and can be severe, while tree-nut allergies may include almonds. Someone with a diagnosed allergy should follow their medical guidance rather than treating one nut as a casual substitute for another. Cross-contact warnings also matter for packaged foods. For people without allergies, peanuts are often one of the least expensive ways to obtain the nutritional benefits associated with nuts.

A mixed approach is perfectly reasonable: peanuts for affordable protein and snacking, almonds for variety and vitamin E, and other nuts or seeds for different fatty acids and minerals. Dietary diversity usually offers more value than trying to identify a single “healthiest” nut.

Mineral absorption is another small distinction. Both foods contain phytate, which can reduce absorption of minerals such as iron and zinc to some degree. Roasting, soaking, and the overall composition of the diet influence that effect. In a varied diet with adequate intake, this is rarely a reason to avoid either food. The larger nutritional question remains whether the snack replaces less nutritious options and fits energy needs.

faq.question: Which has more protein, peanuts or almonds?
faq.answer: Peanuts slightly: about 23.2 versus 21.5 g/100 g in the current raw references.

faq.question: Which has more calcium?
faq.answer: Almonds by a wide margin: about 254 versus 49 mg/100 g.

faq.question: Which has more calories?
faq.answer: They are close at equal portions; about 165 versus 175 calories per 30 g in these references.
